records.toxicity_detail: Toxic to pets. Penn State Extension names Hyacinthus orientalis specifically, stating that in addition to symptoms similar to those from consuming daffodils, hyacinth toxins can cause depression and tremors, and (in a general note about the forced spring bulbs discussed on that page, including hyacinth) that the bulb carries the highest concentration of toxins. UGA Cooperative Extension's pet-toxicity lists corroborate: ingestion can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and tremors, and classify hyacinth (Hyacinthus spp.) toxicity as "Minor Toxicity, Dermatitis." NC State Extension separately tags this species a problem for cats, dogs, and horses, and RHS labels it a skin irritant specifically to pets ("Pets: Skin irritant").

is_houseplant set to false on NC State Extension's explicit statement that hyacinth is "unsuited to long-term growth in a home" despite being sold as a florist plant. Flagging a tension: RHS's own species-specific "Suggested planting locations and garden types" list for Hyacinthus orientalis includes "Houseplants" -- a tag notably absent from RHS's Narcissus pseudonarcissus (daffodil) page, so it is not generic boilerplate. However RHS's own cultivation prose for this species only describes protecting container plants from frost and "specially treated bulbs" being forced for early indoor flowering -- a seasonal forcing cycle, not sustained indoor growth -- so it does not itself assert long-term houseplant suitability the way NC State's sentence explicitly denies it.

toxicity_detail / toxic plant part: NC State Extension's structured "Poison Part" list (bark, flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds, stems, plus the note "Bulbs contain the highest amount of toxin") sits explicitly under that page's "Poisonous to Humans" heading, not a pet-specific section, so it was not used to support toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail. The bulb-concentration claim used instead comes from Penn State Extension's pet-specific "Spring Holiday Plants and Pets" page, which states it as a general note about the forced spring bulbs discussed there (crocus, daffodil, hyacinth, tulip) rather than as a hyacinth-exclusive statement -- no admissible source states bulb-concentration as a hyacinth-specific, pets-specific fact on its own.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The unknowns text resolves an apparent conflict (NC State: "unsuited to long-term growth in a home" vs. an alleged RHS "Houseplants" tag in its species-specific planting-locations list) entirely through the researcher's own prose reasoning, but no citation entry in the array actually quotes RHS's "Houseplants" tag or any RHS planting-locations list -- it's asserted, not sourced. Per the audit's disagreement rule, a real cross-source conflict on a field should either be cited properly on both sides or leave the field null; here an uncited claim about the 'losing' source was used to rationalize away the conflict instead.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The value "moderate" doesn't clearly derive from either supporting quote. Citation 11 (NC State) only warns "Bulb rot may occur in poorly drained soils" -- a caution against poor drainage, implying a need for good/sharp drainage, not literally "moderate." Citation 12 (RHS) says "Grow in moderately fertile soil with good drainage" -- the word "moderately" there modifies fertility, not drainage; drainage itself is described plainly as "good." Neither quote supports a "moderate" drainage characterization specifically; if anything both point toward a well-drained/sharp-drainage need.

name_note — removed on audit: The note asserts "RHS explicitly marks 'Name Status Correct' for this binomial," but no citation entry in the array contains that quote or any RHS text about name status -- citation 1 (the only scientific-name citation) is from NC State, and the two RHS citations present (8, 12, covering sun exposure and soil drainage) never mention name status. This is a specific factual claim about a source that isn't traceable to anything in the citations array, even though the underlying conclusion (Hyacinthus orientalis being the currently accepted name) happens to be correct.

records.name_note: RHS lists Name Status as "Correct" for Crocus vernus, with synonyms Crocus albiflorus, Crocus pictus 'Pictus', Crocus vernus subsp. albiflorus, and Crocus vernus subsp. vernus. RHS also confirms the family as Iridaceae. This is the true crocus (Iridaceae), a genus and family taxonomically distinct from Colchicum autumnale ("autumn crocus," Colchicaceae), which is already catalogued separately; no toxicity, care, or naming data about Colchicum was used for this record.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: no admissible source gives an unambiguous pet-toxicity determination. RHS's 'Potentially harmful' section for this exact species page reads: 'Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers.' Unlike this catalog's other confirmed-toxic ornamentals (Oleander, Easter Lily, Sago Palm), all of which use RHS's explicit 'TOXIC to pets if eaten' wording, this Crocus vernus page never uses the word 'toxic' -- only a generic 'ornamental bulb, not to be eaten' handling caution that RHS appears to apply broadly across many spring-bulb genera. Missouri Botanical Garden's 'Problems' section for this species covers only rodent/squirrel corm predation ('No serious insect or disease problems. Squirrels, mice and other rodents can be problems... Deer tend to avoid crocus.') with no poisoning language, and NC State's crocus profile carries no 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' or 'Poisonous' tags at all. Given the task's explicit warning not to let Colchicum autumnale's severe toxicity leak into this genuinely distinct genus, and given the RHS text's own weaker, non-'TOXIC' phrasing, toxic_to_pets was left null rather than inferred true from an ambiguous generic bulb-handling disclaimer.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source states day or night temperature targets; every source treats Crocus vernus exclusively as an outdoor garden/naturalizing corm, never as a temperature-controlled indoor or forced plant.

chill_damage_f: only survival/hardiness-zone data exists, not a damage-onset figure -- RHS gives Hardiness H6 ('hardy in all of UK and northern Europe', -20 to -15°C), Missouri Botanical Garden gives 'Zone: 3 to 8', and NC State lists USDA zones '3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, 5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b'. These are winter-survival hardiness ratings, not a specific temperature at which cold damage begins, so per the field's own definition (damage-onset, not survival) this was left null.
cool_rest_note: no admissible source frames winter dormancy as a deliberate temperature-based rest step; it is described only as ordinary seasonal corm dormancy with foliage die-back.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source for this outdoor garden corm.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives footcandle figures. A specific sun-hours figure (2-6 hours for partial shade) appears only on NC State's 'Species Crocuses' page, which is explicitly a genus-wide profile ('Common crocus is a genus in the Iridaceae... comprising about 90 species'), not a Crocus vernus-specific page -- it illustrates several species (C. imperati, C. longiflorus, C. chrysanthus, C. tomasini) with C. vernus appearing only as one of many photo captions among others. Because the two species-specific sources (RHS, MOBOT) that support outdoor_sun_exposure give only categorical full_sun/part_shade descriptions with no hours figure, and because a prior audit in this catalog (Sago Palm, b19-toxic-ornamentals) flagged exactly this pattern -- presenting a genus-level hours figure alongside an unconditional full_sun value implies a cap the sources don't actually state -- direct_sun_hours_max was left null rather than borrowed from the genus-wide page.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: RHS gives only the categorical tolerance 'pH: Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' with no numeric bound; no other admissible source states a pH figure for this species.

soil_drainage: classified as 'fast' based on RHS's plain 'Moisture: Well–drained' (no moisture-retentive qualifier, unlike some other bulbs' 'Moist but well-drained' phrasing) and MOBOT's explicit 'Plants perform best in gritty, well-drained soils. Avoid heavy clay soils or moist soil conditions.' Note MOBOT's separate structured field reads 'Water: Medium' rather than 'Low' -- this is read as an average irrigation-frequency rating (a different axis from soil-drainage class) rather than a contradiction of the fast-drainage soil preference, consistent with the explicit prose warning against wet/heavy soils.

water_regime and the water_* estimate fields: left null on a genuine tension between sources' framing of moisture needs. NC State's genus-wide page states 'They tolerate drought, but keep them moist during the growing season' (implying keep_moist), while Missouri Botanical Garden's species-specific culture note states 'Plants perform best in gritty, well-drained soils. Avoid heavy clay soils or moist soil conditions' and separately 'Watering should be reduced as plants go dormant in late spring, with dryish soils generally considered best during dormancy' (implying an overall drier regime with an explicit warning against moist conditions). This is exactly the kind of harm-adjacent field the task instructs not to resolve by picking a side. No source gives a watering-frequency interval in days, a moisture check-depth, or a dormancy-duration estimate, so water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis were also left null.
fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no admissible source discusses fertilizing this species.

is_houseplant: set false by default; no admissible source describes or supports growing Crocus vernus indoors or in containers long-term -- every source treats it exclusively as an outdoor, ground-planted, naturalizing spring corm (lawns, borders, rock and woodland gardens).

is_houseplant — removed on audit: is_houseplant:false is set with zero supporting entries in the citations array — no claim label anywhere in the array even mentions is_houseplant, which fails structural check 1 outright (every non-null field value must trace to at least one citation). The only support offered is prose in `unknowns` asserting 'no admissible source describes or supports growing Crocus vernus indoors or in containers long-term -- every source treats it exclusively as an outdoor, ground-planted, naturalizing spring corm.' A live fetch of the record's own cited RHS page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/29659/crocus-vernus/details) shows its 'Suggested planting locations' section reads verbatim: 'City and courtyard gardens, Cottage and informal garden, Patio and container plants, Wildlife gardens, Wildflower meadow, Banks and slopes, Flower borders and beds' -- RHS explicitly lists 'Patio and container plants' as a suggested use for this exact species, directly contradicting the record's blanket claim that no source supports container growing. This is the identical defect pattern already caught and corrected twice in this same catalog for directly analogous spring bulbs in b20-common-ornamentals.json: Common Garden Tulip's is_houseplant:false was 'removed on audit' because 'the well-known practice of forcing tulip bulbs to bloom indoors in pots is never mentioned' and the record 'conflates grown outdoors and replaced annually with not a houseplant'; Daffodil's is_houseplant:false was likewise 'removed on audit' because 'no entry in the citations array addresses indoor/houseplant status at all,' explicitly citing structural check 1. Forcing crocus corms indoors in pots for a winter/early-spring bloom is at least as well-documented a horticultural practice as forcing tulips or daffodils, so the same reasoning applies with equal or greater force here. Per the catalog's own established precedent, this field should be null, not false.

records.name_note: scientific_name_given and scientific_name_accepted are both kept at the genus level, Hippeastrum, which RHS's own genus profile explicitly marks "Name Status: Correct." NC State's page specifically warns that "the common name Amaryllis is applied both to Hippeastrum species, which are the commonly cultivated bulbs discussed here, and to the genus Amaryllis, which is less commonly cultivated (and comprises only two species native to South Africa)" -- this record is about Hippeastrum, the genus every citation below actually describes. NC State also notes Hippeastrum was "Previously known as: Callicore Leopoldia." The large-flowered bulbs sold each fall as potted "amaryllis" are complex hybrids -- UF/IFAS names them specifically "Hippeastrum x hybridum," and RHS's own growing-guide quick-facts list the botanical name as "Hippeastrum species and cultivars" -- but since NC State, Clemson, and RHS's genus and cultivar pages all document care and toxicity information at or above the genus level rather than isolating one hybrid binomial, no single species/hybrid name was asserted as more "accepted" than the genus name itself.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State lists Hippeastrum as a "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses." Its toxic-principle detail (filed on the page under a subsection literally headed "Poisonous to Humans:", though the text itself names pets) identifies the toxin as "Alkaloid lycorine" and states: "Toxic if eaten in large quantities. Vomiting, salvation, diarrhea; large ingestions cause convulsions, low blood pressure, tremors, and cardiac arrhythmias. Bulbs are the most poisonous part. Especially harmful to pets." Clemson Cooperative Extension confirms independently, in its own standalone (non-human-only) "Toxicity" section: "All parts of the amaryllis are poisonous to humans and pets if ingested in large quantities. The bulb is the most toxic part of the plant." RHS separately carries a cultivar-page warning naming pets directly: "Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten." NC State's checkbox-style list of toxic plant parts ("Flowers, Leaves, Stems") does not include the bulb even though the site's own prose calls the bulb the most poisonous part -- the bulb-concentration claim here rests on that prose and on Clemson's independently matching statement, not on NC State's checkbox list.
records.cool_rest_note: After bloom, most sources agree on a period of enforced dormancy: NC State and RHS both describe moving the bulb to a cool, dim spot -- NC State: "a cool (50 to 55 degrees F), semi-dark location to rest... dormant for 8 to 10 weeks"; RHS: "keep cooler at about 13°C (55°F) for eight to ten weeks," stopping feeding and reducing watering -- before returning it to warmth and light to restart growth. UMD Extension describes a distinct, cooler and shorter rest instead -- "a cool (40-50 degrees F.), dry location" for "about 6-8 weeks" -- so the exact temperature and duration vary somewhat by source.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no source frames temperature by day vs. night. Multiple different ambient-temperature figures appear across sources for different phases/contexts: RHS's growing guide gives 'a well-lit spot at 21°C (70°F)' for initial growth vs. 'about 15–18°C (60-65°F)' once flowering to extend bloom life; the same 15-18°C range is separately described on an RHS cultivar page as 'ideally...desirable for good growth' generally (not phase-specific); Clemson gives 70-75°F for growth and 65°F to prolong bloom; UF/IFAS Circular 1243/EP060 gives 75-80°F for growth. None of these are framed as 'daytime' specifically, and the numbers disagree with each other by phase and by source, so none was mapped onto day_f/night_f.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no source gives a footcandle figure; only categorical sun-position descriptions (full sun/partial shade/part sun) were found.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's own 'Partial Shade' category upper bound (6 hours) is defined only for that category, while its 'Full Sun' category is open-ended ('6 or more hours'); applying the partial-shade figure as a flat ceiling would misleadingly cap full-sun exposure too -- the exact failure mode already documented in this catalog's audited Sago Palm record -- so left null.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State's structured Soil pH field lists all three categories together (Acid <6.0, Neutral 6.0-8.0, Alkaline >8.0), and RHS's 'Bestseller' cultivar page similarly lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- both describe broad tolerance rather than a specific target range, so no defensible numeric min/max exists.

water_regime and its dependent fields (water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis): genuine cross-source conflict on this harm-adjacent field. RHS ('Do not let the compost dry out'), NC State ('moist but with good drainage'), and UF/IFAS EP060 ('Keep soil moist during times of growth and flowering') all describe continuous moisture without a dry-down step, while UMD ('Allow the top 1/2 inch of the soil dry out between waterings') and Clemson ('Watering the plant when the soil surface feels dry to the touch is best') both describe an explicit surface dry-down-before-watering cycle. Per the task's guidance on harm-capable fields, this was left null with both sides documented rather than picking one.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: Clemson gives 'twice a month' and RHS gives 'weekly' (aftercare regrowth phase) -- both frequency words, and per this catalog's established policy the only permitted word-to-number translation is a named month to its calendar number for fertilize_active_months, not a frequency word to a day-count, so these were left null. No source names specific calendar months or a liquid-fertilizer dilution strength (full/half/quarter) either.

cool_rest_note: NC State and RHS closely agree (cool 50-55°F / about 55°F, semi-dark, 8-10 weeks) but UMD describes a distinct, cooler and shorter rest (40-50°F for about 6-8 weeks); both figures are represented in the note rather than presenting either as the single answer.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail structural note: NC State's detailed Poison Severity/Toxic Principle fields are technically filed on the page under a subsection literally headed 'Poisonous to Humans:' -- however, the Poison Symptoms sentence within that same block explicitly states 'Especially harmful to pets,' and NC State's separate 'Problems:' tag list (not nested under that heading) independently flags 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' and 'Problem for Horses.' Clemson's toxicity statement is a standalone section not nested under any human-only heading and explicitly names both humans and pets, and RHS's 'Bestseller' cultivar page has its own dedicated 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten' line -- so toxic_to_pets rests on three independent sources, not solely on the human-labeled NC State block.

toxicity_detail bulb-concentration note: NC State's checkbox-style 'Poison Part' field lists only 'Flowers, Leaves, Stems' and does not include 'Bulb' as a tagged part, even though the adjacent Poison Symptoms prose states 'Bulbs are the most poisonous part.' The bulb-concentration claim in toxicity_detail relies on that prose sentence and on Clemson's independent, matching statement ('The bulb is the most toxic part of the plant'), not on NC State's checkbox list.

UGA C1245 exclusion: this source lists an entry for 'Amaryllis spp.' (Minor Toxicity, Dermatitis) rather than 'Hippeastrum.' NC State's own page explicitly warns that the common name 'Amaryllis' is used both for Hippeastrum (documented here) and for a separate South African genus Amaryllis, and NC State separately states Hippeastrum 'Causes Contact Dermatitis: No' -- the opposite of UGA's 'Dermatitis' toxicity class -- consistent with UGA's entry describing the other genus. This record therefore does not cite UGA C1245 as pet-toxicity evidence for Hippeastrum. The same genus-name ambiguity applies to a UGA CAES Field Report holiday-plants article ('Amaryllis – the bulbs and seeds') that was likewise not cited for this reason.

Missouri Botanical Garden: plantfinder.mobot.org's Hippeastrum page could not be retrieved (a TLS certificate error on direct fetch and a bot-detection block in the browser), so it was not used as a source for this record.

outdoor_sun_exposure full_sun nuance: two UF/IFAS sources describe a trade-off around full sun exposure -- FP255 says foliage 'will discolor when plants are grown in full sun, although they will flower better,' and a second UF/IFAS circular (EP060) says the plant 'does best in light shade' and that 'leaves may yellow in full sun.' full_sun is still included because NC State and RHS's cultivar page both list it as a plain structured position category without qualification, but this foliage/flowering trade-off is noted here rather than silently dropped.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The 'part_sun' member of this array rests solely on UF/IFAS FP255's Culture field, which I confirmed via raw HTML is a single continuous prose value -- 'Light requirement: plant grows in part shade/part sun' -- not two independently checked categories the way NC State's Light field displays 'Full sun' and 'Partial Shade' as separate structured <dd> entries. No other admissible source (NC State: full sun/partial shade only; RHS Bestseller: full sun/partial shade only) independently names 'part sun' as a category distinct from 'part shade.' Treating one ambiguous compound descriptor from a single source as confirmation of two separate categorical tags overstates what that source establishes, so the 'part_sun' value is not solidly supported even though 'full_sun' and 'part_shade' are fine.

records.name_note: This record profiles the genus Brugmansia as a single entry, matching NC State Extension's own plant-profile page, which is titled simply "Brugmansia" with no Species field populated ("Angel's trumpet is a genus of seven species of tropical evergreen shrub or small tree..."). UF/IFAS's EP648 confirms Brugmansia is the currently accepted genus name and clarifies its relationship to the similarly toxic but distinct genus Datura, which this record deliberately does not draw on: "Angel's trumpet was once included in the genus Datura but is recognized now in its own genus, Brugmansia," and that genus "consists of seven species and several hybrids." No admissible source disputes Brugmansia as the accepted genus, and none of the admissible sources anchors this entry to a single accepted species-level binomial within the genus, so scientific_name_accepted is set to the genus name "Brugmansia" to match scientific_name_given, consistent with how NC State Extension itself catalogs this plant.
records.cool_rest_note: Brugmansia is a tender tropical that is normally overwintered indoors or in frost-free storage rather than left outside. Reduce watering to occasional once the plant is no longer in active growth; RHS states most species need a minimum night temperature of about 45-50°F (7-10°C) and a day temperature of about 50-54°F (10-12°C) during winter storage. Resume normal watering and feeding (organic liquid seaweed feed, then a high-potassium fertiliser for flowering) once new growth begins in spring.
records.water_dry_down_target: Check the compost/potting mix daily since it can dry out very quickly; water as needed to avoid letting it dry out completely, but avoid letting the pot become waterlogged.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: left null. No admissible source gives a general ambient day/night temperature preference for the actively growing plant. The only Fahrenheit figures found (RHS's 'minimum night temperature of 7-10C (45-50F) and day temperature of 10-12C (50-54F)') describe winter dormant storage specifically, not general growing comfort, so they were used for cool_rest_note instead of these fields.

chill_damage_f: left null. RHS's genus page states plants must be 'kept above 7-10C (45-50F) over winter, as this tropical plant can't tolerate winter cold,' and its growing guide repeats the same 45-50F/50-54F figures as the winter-storage minimum. Both are framed as a survival/dormancy threshold ('can't tolerate...', 'minimum...needed'), not an explicit damage-onset statement (no 'injury/leaf drop occurs below X' language as seen for other species in this catalog), so per instructions distinguishing damage-onset from survival ratings this was not mapped to chill_damage_f.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: left null. No admissible source addresses ambient humidity requirements for this genus.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: left null. No admissible source gives a foot-candle light measurement.

direct_sun_hours_max: left null. NC State's tag 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' defines the minimum threshold for its Full-sun category, not a maximum for this plant, and no source gives an upper hour limit.

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_sun was deliberately excluded despite mixed evidence. NC State's own page contains an internal conflict: its categorical Light tags list both 'Full sun' and 'Partial Shade,' but its own descriptive prose states plainly, in a complete sentence with full surrounding context: 'It does best when there is a lot of room for roots to grow. Do not put the plant in full sun. Angel's Trumpet grows best when using lots of seasoned water...' RHS's species-level pages for two Brugmansia species (arborea: 'Full sun, Partial shade'; suaveolens: 'Full sun') do support full_sun, and RHS's genus growing guide says the outdoor summer position can be 'partial shade or sun' -- so evidence is genuinely mixed both within and across admissible sources. Given the direct same-source self-contradiction on NC State's own page, full_sun was excluded and only part_shade (agreed on by every source checked) was kept.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: left null. No admissible source gives a numeric soil pH for this genus.
water_check_depth_cm: left null. RHS's guidance describes checking 'the compost' generally, not a specific check depth.

water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: left null. No admissible source gives a specific day-count watering interval; RHS describes watering 'as needed' during growth (checked daily by feel) and 'only occasionally' in winter dormancy, but gives no exact day-count figure for either.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: left null. RHS's growing guide names only 'spring' (seaweed feed) and 'summer' (high-potassium feed) without specific calendar months or a day interval, and defers dilution strength to 'the dose rate and frequency recommended on the packaging' rather than stating one itself.

toxicity_detail human vs. pet distinction: NC State's and UF/IFAS's detailed symptom lists (hallucinations, dry mouth, dilated pupils, etc.) are both filed under human-poisoning-specific data (NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' section; UF/IFAS's Florida poisonous-landscape-plants publication, framed around human/child poisoning risk) and were not used to support toxic_to_pets. That field instead rests separately on RHS's explicit 'TOXIC to pets' tag.

toxic_to_pets sourcing note: this record profiles the genus Brugmansia as a whole (matching NC State's own genus-level profile, which has no Species field). NC State's genus page itself carries only a 'Poisonous to Humans' / 'Problem for Children' tag, with no dedicated pet-toxicity tag. toxic_to_pets=true instead rests on RHS's structured 'TOXIC to pets' tag, found consistently on three separate RHS pages for named species/cultivars within this exact genus (B. arborea, B. suaveolens, B. x candida 'Grand Marnier') -- i.e. species-specific evidence for members of the very genus being catalogued, not an inference drawn from a broader family-level statement. No admissible source disputes pet toxicity for any Brugmansia species/cultivar checked.

water_regime: mapped to keep_moist from RHS's growing-guide instruction to 'check the compost daily, as it can dry out very quickly' and 'water as needed to avoid letting it dry out completely,' combined with its separate statement that the plant dislikes waterlogged conditions. This is derived from a single admissible source describing container culture specifically; no admissible source addresses garden-bed/in-ground watering practice for this genus.

Two UF/IFAS-domain pages surfaced during search but were confirmed NOT usable and were not cited: 'FP077' (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/FP077) is actually about the unrelated genus Brunfelsia, not Brugmansia -- checked directly and excluded to avoid a genus-confusion error of exactly the kind flagged for Datura. Separately, hort.ifas.ufl.edu (a different, non-admissible IFAS subdomain from the approved edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ask.ifas.ufl.edu) hosts dedicated Brugmansia fact sheets that were not used because that subdomain is outside the admissible source list.

Genus vs. species scope: per UF/IFAS EP648, 'Brugmansia consists of seven species and several hybrids'; this record profiles the genus collectively (as NC State Extension's own single plant-profile page does) rather than any one of the seven species, so field values reflect genus-wide statements plus, where noted, corroborating species-specific RHS data for named members of the genus.

is_houseplant is supported for the genus generally; no admissible source distinguishes which of the seven species specifically tolerate sustained indoor culture year-round versus only being brought indoors seasonally for winter protection.

Clemson HGIC (hgic.clemson.edu) and University of Maryland Extension (extension.umd.edu) were both searched specifically for Brugmansia/Angel's Trumpet content. Clemson's only hit was a one-line mention in a 'Growing Annuals' factsheet listing 'Angel's Trumpet (Brugmansia species)' under fragrant annuals with no care detail. UMD's 'EB314 - 100 Poisonous Plants of Maryland' PDF was located and fetched but its content was not machine-readable (rendered as corrupted/binary text), so no usable Brugmansia entry could be confirmed or quoted from it. UGA Cooperative Extension's 'Landscape Plants for Georgia' (B625) publication does not include Brugmansia at all.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Direct fetch of the cited pages confirms NC State's alkaloid/symptom data sits explicitly under a 'Poisonous to Humans' heading, and UF/IFAS EP648's alkaloid and symptom sentences come from a publication framed around human/child poisoning risk -- exactly the human-toxicity-section content structural check 3 asks to screen out of an animal-facing toxicity_detail field. The record's own text discloses this framing honestly, but disclosure doesn't cure the overreach: citations 10-13, which supply the bulk of the field's specific content (severity rating, named alkaloids, the multi-symptom list), are not animal-toxicity content and are not rescued by independent corroboration the way is_houseplant/soil_base were -- removing them leaves only thin general statements ('highly poisonous,' 'poisonous if eaten, especially seeds and leaves' from citations 14-15). No admissible source supplies an actual animal-specific mechanism or symptom list; the only genuinely pet-specific evidence anywhere in this record is the bare, unelaborated 'TOXIC to pets' tag on three RHS species pages, which is used for toxic_to_pets but doesn't license the detailed human-sourced narrative presented under toxicity_detail.

So no admissible citation directly and cleanly supports 'Agave americana' (unranked) as the accepted name; the record gets there only via its own inserted botanical argument (subsp. americana is the autonym, so it isn't a conflict), which is the researcher's inference, not something any of the three quotes states. records.name_note: "Water Lily" as commonly sold is not tied to one accepted binomial; admissible sources default to genus- or hybrid-group-level treatment rather than a single species. NC State Extension's genus overview states water lilies are "a group of aquatic plants containing about 70 species in the waterlily family (Nymphaeaceae)" and covers the material across three separate group pages ("Hardy Water Lilies," "Tropical Day Blooming Water Lilies," "Tropical Night Blooming Water Lilies") rather than one species page. Clemson's aquatic-plant-selection factsheet frames both groups the same way -- "Hardy water lilies (Nymphaea species and cultivars)" and "Tropical water lilies (Nymphaea species and cultivars, such as N. capensis, N. colorata, N. gigantea, N. lotus, and N. rubra)" -- naming several component tropical species without singling one out as "the" water lily. RHS's own genus page (common names "sea rose, water lily") is likewise genus-level with no accepted-binomial designation. The one admissible source with a single-species title, UF/IFAS's FPS434/FP434 "Nymphaea odorata Fragrant Water Lily," could not be retrieved (both edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fp434 and its ask.ifas.ufl.edu redirect returned HTTP 410 Gone -- see unknowns), so it does not establish N. odorata as the sole referent either, and would in any case be only one native species among the many hardy and tropical species/hybrids commonly sold as "water lily." Given this, scientific_name_given is recorded as the genus "Nymphaea," and scientific_name_accepted is left null rather than narrowed to one binomial.
records.cool_rest_note: Hardy types need no winter protection -- cut back the dying foliage in late autumn and leave the dormant rootstock in the pond, where it survives as long as the water doesn't freeze solid. Tropical types can't take a hard freeze: keep the pond water at a minimum of 50°F (10°C) over winter, or lift the tubers, remove the foliage, and store them in damp sand in the dark at roughly 50-55°F until spring.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: no admissible source addresses toxicity to pets (or humans) for Nymphaea/water lily. None of the three NC State Extension group pages checked (Hardy Water Lilies; Tropical Day Blooming Water Lilies; Tropical Night Blooming Water Lilies) carries a 'Problems'/poison-tag section of the kind NC State uses elsewhere to flag 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses.' RHS's genus page and its Nymphaea alba and 'Pygmaea Helvola' species pages were checked directly and carry no toxicity/harmful/pets section either. UGA CAES Field Report's two pet-toxic-plant list articles ('These 25+ plants are toxic to pets' and 'Keep these toxic plants away from your pets') do not include water lily or Nymphaea among their listed plants. Absence of a flag is not the same as an admissible source affirmatively stating the plant is non-toxic, so both fields are left null rather than set to false, per instructions not to infer toxicity from genus/family.

day_f_min, day_f_max, night_f_min, night_f_max: left null. The only ambient-temperature figures found -- NC State's tropical-page note that tropical water lilies 'prefer temperatures above 70 degrees F so don't plant them too early in the spring,' and MOBOT's statement that tropical water lilies thrive once 'the air temperature reaches a stable 70°F, and the water temperature is at least 70°F' -- describe a seasonal safe-to-plant-outdoors threshold specific to tropical-type Nymphaea, not a general ambient day/night comfort range, and don't apply to hardy types at all, so were not mapped onto these fields.

chill_damage_f: left null -- a genuine conflict on a harm-capable field between the two subtypes sold as 'Water Lily.' RHS states tropical waterlilies 'need a water temperature of at least 10˚C (50˚F) over winter,' implying damage/death below that. MOBOT states hardy water lilies' 'rootstock can survive cold water, as long as the water does not freeze solid' -- a far lower, unquantified threshold. Recording 50°F as a single value would misrepresent hardy plants as damaged at a temperature they actually tolerate, so the field is left null; both figures are captured, correctly scoped by type, in cool_rest_note instead.

But Penn State Extension's Mid-Atlantic Pocket Guide gives Nymphaea odorata specifically a 'Water Quality Needs' value of 'Somewhat acidic' -- the opposite direction from MOBOT's neutral-to-alkaline figure. humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient air humidity for this species -- consistent with it being an aquatic plant whose rhizome/tuber sits submerged in pond water with leaves floating on the surface, a growing context none of the admissible sources frame in humidity terms.

soil_base: left null. This is an aquatic pond plant grown in a submerged planting basket, not a container of ordinary potting mix or an in-ground garden bed, and none of the fixed enum values (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, ericaceous, orchid_bark, african_violet, semi_hydro, garden_bed) describes that setup without misrepresenting it. Admissible sources instead describe the medium directly: MOBOT recommends 'a weighted material such as a clay loam garden soil' and warns 'soilless mediums such as peat moss, bark, or those containing perlite are not recommended because the material will float'; RHS's growing guide specifies 'peat-free aquatic compost or heavy clay-based loam, in an aquatic basket'; NC State recommends 'heavier clay soil to prevent it from floating' in containers; UF/IFAS's FP436 (for the hardy hybrid 'Attraction') specifies a 'container filled with garden soil or potting mix' amended with 'one-fifth well-decomposed cow manure.'

soil_drainage: left null. NC State tags this genus 'Frequent Standing Water,' meaning permanently submerged/waterlogged conditions, which none of the fixed enum values (fast, moderate, moisture_retentive) accurately captures without forcing an awkward fit.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: left null. These fields assume a container plant cycling between wet and dry (or moist and barely-moist) conditions; Nymphaea's rhizome/tuber instead sits permanently submerged and is never allowed to dry out, so the premise behind these fields doesn't apply. Admissible sources do give substantial pond-planting-depth data this schema has no field for: MOBOT states 'the depth of the water above water lily plant crowns should be at least 6 inches deep; 8–10 inches is preferable'; RHS's growing guide gives depth by cultivar size -- dwarf cultivars need water '30–45cm (12–18in) deep,' medium '45–75cm (18–30in) deep,' large '75–120cm (30in–4ft) deep'; UF/IFAS's FP436 states the hardy hybrid 'Attraction' 'grows in standing water about 18 inches deep.' None of this is a soil-surface check depth on a drying-out container, so it was not force-mapped onto water_check_depth_cm.

fertilize_interval_days: left null. MOBOT gives two different values for the two subtypes sold under this common name: 'Hardy water lilies should be fed once a month, while tropical water lilies are typically fed once every two weeks' (~30 days vs. ~14 days) -- a genuine split not resolved by picking one.

fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a liquid-feed dilution strength (full/half/quarter). UF/IFAS's FP436 gives a specific granular dose -- 'one-quarter cup 10-10-10 per gallon of soil' -- but that is a soil-amendment ratio at planting time, not a feed-dilution strength, so it wasn't force-mapped onto this enum.

scientific_name_accepted: left null -- see name_note for the full genus/hybrid-group framing. UF/IFAS's FPS434/FP434 ('Nymphaea odorata Fragrant Water Lily') is the one admissible source with a single-species title, but it could not be retrieved: https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fp434 redirects to https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/fp434, and both that URL and https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/FP434 returned HTTP 410 Gone.

Penn State Extension was also checked at 'Types of Aquatic Plants and Algae' and 'Tips for Creating a Water Garden' -- both mention water lily only in passing ('Water lily has large leaves and is an ideal habitat for fish and aquatic insects') with no numeric cultivation data beyond what's already cited from the Mid-Atlantic Pocket Guide.

UMD Extension's 'White Water Lily' resource page was checked but its visible page text gives no cultivation data (sun, depth, soil, fertilizing) for Nymphaea odorata beyond noting it is grown 'in ornamental ponds or small ponds for the purpose of esthetics' and can spread to 'completely cut off the surface' if uncontrolled; a linked PDF may hold more detail but was not part of the fetched page content.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The record sets this to an empty string "" rather than JSON null, even though name_note and the unknowns entry both frame the decision explicitly as leaving the field 'null' (e.g. 'scientific_name_accepted is left null rather than narrowed to one binomial'). The underlying research justification is genuinely sound -- I independently confirmed edis.ifas.ufl.edu/fp434 301-redirects to ask.ifas.ufl.edu/fp434, which returns HTTP 410 Gone, and confirmed the RHS, NC State, and Clemson sources really do treat water lilies at genus/hybrid-group level with no single accepted binomial -- but the stored value doesn't match the documented convention. An empty string is a populated-but-empty value, not the same sentinel as the null used everywhere else in this record for un-established fields, and downstream code that distinguishes 'no data' (null) from 'field explicitly checked and empty' ("") will misclassify this record.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: ninth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Three more toxic bulbs/ornamentals confirmed toxic_to_pets=true (Hyacinth, Amaryllis, Angel's Trumpet -- the last one is one of the most toxic ornamentals commonly grown, tropane alkaloids), completing the true Crocus (Iridaceae) as a deliberate companion record to Autumn Crocus (Colchicum autumnale, Colchicaceae, already in this catalog from b19) -- the two are frequently confused by common name but taxonomically unrelated and very differently toxic; this record correctly declined to let Colchicum's severe toxicity leak in, and just as correctly declined to invent a toxic_to_pets=true from RHS's weaker 'not to be eaten' bulb-handling boilerplate, landing an honest null instead. Rounded out with Century Plant, Liriope, Raspberry (completing a bramble-fruit trio with blackberry and blueberry), and Water Lily (this catalog's first true aquatic pond plant, correctly recorded at genus level -- "water lily" as commonly sold isn't tied to one accepted binomial, and every admissible source treats it that way).

The audit caught a real, subtle citation-and-precedent gap on Crocus vernus: is_houseplant was set false with zero supporting citation, and a live fetch found RHS's own page for this exact species lists 'Patio and container plants' among its suggested uses -- directly contradicting the record's blanket claim. The audit explicitly named this the same defect already caught twice in b20 for Tulip and Daffodil (forcing spring bulbs indoors in pots is a well-documented practice), holding this record to the catalog's own established precedent rather than judging it in isolation.

Century Plant (Agave americana) surfaced a genuinely subtle taxonomic-rank mismatch: the only citation offering a formal name-status determination is RHS's page for 'Agave americana subsp. americana' specifically (an infraspecific rank), not the unranked binomial the record wrote into scientific_name_accepted -- the record's own inserted botanical argument (autonym convention) is probably correct in fact but isn't something any cited quote states, so both the field and its supporting name_note were nulled on a traceability failure rather than a factual one.

One schema bug this batch, caught and self-corrected by the auditor itself (no manual fix needed): Water Lily's scientific_name_accepted was written as an empty string instead of JSON null, even though the record's own name_note and unknowns text both already said 'left null' -- the auditor named this specific format defect as its own finding, which the batch script's cleanup step then correctly nulled.
